name: Preppy / Ivy style

lead: Preppy, or Ivy, style grew from the clothing of Northeastern prep schools and Ivy League campuses. Oxford shirts, chinos, loafers and navy blazers are its core pieces.
It is discussed in appearance communities as a clean, classic dress option. No research has tested its effect on perceived attractiveness.

paras: Wearers choose structured, traditional garments and a coordinated, conservative palette. The style carries class associations that the original preppy literature itself satirised.
No health risks are documented. Cost depends on brand choices.

lead: Preppy is a style of dress associated with graduates of Northeastern US college-preparatory schools and with upper-class and old-money backgrounds.[1] Its menswear root, Ivy style, began in the early 1900s and was widespread by the late 1950s, named for Ivy League campuses.[1]
Typical staples include navy blazers, Oxford cloth button-down shirts, repp stripe ties, chinos, penny loafers, polo shirts and boat shoes.[1]
No published studies have tested whether preppy or Ivy dress changes how attractive a person is judged to be.

paras: The look draws on sailing, rowing and golf clothing and on British country wear such as tweed jackets and brogues.[1] Over time it became more relaxed, adding rugby shirts and boat shoes, with outfitters such as L.L. Bean, Eddie Bauer and Orvis supplying casual items.[1]
Fabrics and patterns commonly named include seersucker, madras and Nantucket red.[1]

J. Press and Brooks Brothers were key early retailers of Ivy style.[1] Women's preppy-influenced fashion emerged in the 1960s through Seven Sisters college students and designers such as Lilly Pulitzer and Perry Ellis.[1]

Lisa Birnbach's 1980 book The Official Preppy Handbook, a tongue-in-cheek guide to elite campus life, is credited with a 1980s revival, and Ralph Lauren, Lacoste and Izod brought the look to the mass market.[1] Interest declined in the 1990s, though brands such as J. Crew, Tommy Hilfiger and Vineyard Vines remain associated with it.[1]
